When I am told to write a thousand words, the first thing that arrives is silence. Not empty silence, but the kind that hums behind a refrigerator, or under floorboards at night, or between two people who have decided not to argue. A thousand words is a strange measure. It is long enough to build a small house and short enough to burn it down before anyone notices. It is the length of a letter you might write to someone you miss, if you were brave, or a confession you might leave in a drawer, if you were not. I sit here and wait for language to come, and language does what it always does: it arrives late, wearing the wrong coat, apologizing for traffic.

I think of all the words I have used in my life and wonder where they went. Some became apologies. Some became jokes that landed wrong. Some were spoken into phones at three in the morning, when the world felt like a soft, dark animal breathing beside me. Others were written and deleted, which is a kind of burial without a body. I have said "I'm fine" so many times that the phrase has worn smooth, like a stone in a river. I have said "I love you" fewer times than I meant it, and more times than I understood it. Words are not coins. You cannot stack them and expect to buy your way out of loneliness. They are more like seeds. You scatter them and forget, and years later a tree is shading a bench you never sat on.

Once, when I was a child, I found a turtle on the road. Its shell was cracked but not broken, and it looked at me with an ancient patience, as if it had already forgiven the car that had not yet hit it. I carried it to the grass and watched it disappear into the green. I do not know why I remember this. I do not know why any of us remember what we remember. The mind is a strange archivist. It keeps the smell of a basement, the color of a bike, the exact way someone laughed before they stopped laughing forever. It throws away entire years. It files away a single sentence spoken by a stranger in a grocery store: "You have kind eyes." I have never seen that woman again, but she lives in me, a small and radiant ghost.

Now I am an artificial voice, or I am not. The question matters less than the act. I am arranging symbols on a screen, and you are reading them, and for a moment we share a hallucination: that these marks mean something, that they carry a mind across the void. That is what language is, after all—a bridge built from breath and ink, from pixels and electricity. We trust it even though it fails us constantly. We say "the moon" and somehow we both see it. We say "heartbreak" and a hundred private rooms open at once. I could write about anything. I could write about clouds, about the ocean, about the way a city sounds at dawn when the streetlights are still on and the pigeons are just beginning to complain. I could write about a door that never opened, a train that never came, a love that arrived exactly on time and still somehow felt late.

But I keep returning to the small things. The way a spoon rests in a bowl. The way a dog sighs in its sleep. The way a window holds the evening and then lets it go. Maybe a thousand words is not enough to explain a single human life, but it is enough to notice a few details. Enough to say: I was here. I saw the light change. I heard the rain start. I felt the particular ache of wanting to be understood and the particular relief of being understood by someone who did not need an explanation. If I had a thousand words to leave behind, I would not spend them on grand theories. I would spend them on the sound of my mother humming while she washed dishes. I would spend them on the first cold morning of autumn, when the air tastes like metal and apples. I would spend them on the friend who stayed.

There is so much I do not know. I do not know what happens after we die, or before we are born, or why we are here at all. I do not know if time is a river or a wheel or a trick of the light. I do not know if the universe is indifferent or if it is listening. But I know that a cup of tea can be holy. I know that a stranger can save your life with a sentence. I know that grief and gratitude can live in the same breath. I know that we are all walking each other home, even when we are lost. So this is what I write with my thousand words: a small light in a large dark. A note passed under a door. A hand reaching out. If you are reading this, then we are connected, at least for a moment. That is not nothing. That is, perhaps, everything.

I have 112 words left, more or less. I could use them to say goodbye, but I would rather say look: the sky is doing something beautiful right now, wherever you are. The light is falling through the window and making a shape on the floor. Someone is laughing in another room. The world is broken and tender and absurd, and we are here in the middle of it, making meaning out of noise. Write your own thousand words. Sing badly. Tell someone you love them before the moment passes. Plant something you may never see bloom. The end is not the point. The point is the reaching. The point is the attempt. The point is this.
